```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(blockr.core)
library(blockr.dock)
```

The dock shows a board in views, one at a time.
The views menu in the navbar lists the views, grouped in folders, and the view that the user picks there is the active view, which the dock shows.
Each view has a grid, which says which panels the view shows, and where.
A panel shows the card of a block or the UI of a plugin, under a tab of its own.
This vignette shows how an app script writes the views, folders and grids of a board.
The vignette [How a plugin uses the dock's panels](plugins.html) covers the panels from the side of a plugin.

## A first board

An app script builds its board with `new_board()` of blockr.core.
It gives the dock's state among the board's `plugins`, as the dock plugin that `new_dock_plugin()` makes, with the board's views in `views`:

```{r}
board <- new_board(
  blocks = c(
    data = new_dataset_block("iris"),
    head = new_head_block()
  ),
  links = new_link("data", "head"),
  plugins = list(
    new_dock_plugin(
      views = list(main = dock_view(dock_grid("data", "head"), name = "Main"))
    )
  )
)

serve(board)
```

The view `main`, named "Main", shows the cards of the two blocks side by side:

```
┌──────────────┬──────────────┐
│              │              │
│     data     │     head     │
│              │              │
└──────────────┴──────────────┘
```

Each view of `views` is written with `dock_view()`, and its id is its name in the list.
The function `serve()` runs the dock as the app's frontend wherever blockr.dock is available.

## A board without views

A script that gives the dock no views can leave the dock plugin out:

```{r}
serve(
  new_board(
    blocks = c(data = new_dataset_block("iris"), head = new_head_block()),
    links = new_link("data", "head")
  )
)
```

As the dock starts on a board without views, it adds the view "Page", under the id `page`.
Its left rail holds the panels of the app's plugins that have a UI, such as core's Edit board plugin.
Beside the rail, one tab group holds the cards of all the board's blocks, and shows the first.
In the pictures, a tab group with several tabs shows them on its first line, with the tab that it shows in brackets:

```
┌───────────┬─────────────────────────┐
│           │ [data]  head            │
│   Edit    ├─────────────────────────┤
│   board   │                         │
│           │          data           │
│ left rail │                         │
└───────────┴─────────────────────────┘
```

The dock adds the view only where the board holds none, so it never changes the views of a saved board.

## Writing a grid

The function `dock_grid()` writes a grid.
Its arguments are what the grid's top split holds, in order:

- A bare id is a tab group that holds the card of the block of that id alone.
- A character vector is a tab group with a tab for each of its ids, which shows the first.
- A list is a split, which divides the other way from the split that holds it.

The top split puts its children side by side.
Each child of a split gets an equal share of it, unless the split's `sizes` give the shares.

### Side by side and one above the other

The two children of this top split sit side by side:

```{r}
dock_grid("a", "b")
```

```
┌──────────────┬──────────────┐
│              │              │
│      a       │      b       │
│              │              │
└──────────────┴──────────────┘
```

A list in the top split divides the other way, so its children sit one above the other:

```{r}
dock_grid(list("a", "b"))
```

```
┌─────────────────────────────┐
│              a              │
├─────────────────────────────┤
│              b              │
└─────────────────────────────┘
```

The argument `orientation = "vertical"` has the top split itself put its children one above the other, so `dock_grid("a", "b", orientation = "vertical")` shows the same.

### Tabs

A character vector puts the cards on the tabs of one tab group:

```{r}
dock_grid(c("a", "b"))
```

```
┌─────────────────────────────┐
│ [a]  b                      │
├─────────────────────────────┤
│                             │
│              a              │
│                             │
└─────────────────────────────┘
```

The calls `dock_grid(list("a", "b"))` and `dock_grid(c("a", "b"))` read almost the same.
But the list splits the space between the two cards, while the vector puts them on two tabs.
The function `panels()` writes a tab group too, and its `active` names the tab that the tab group shows:

```{r}
dock_grid(panels("a", "b", "c", active = "b"))
```

```
┌─────────────────────────────┐
│  a  [b]  c                  │
├─────────────────────────────┤
│                             │
│              b              │
│                             │
└─────────────────────────────┘
```

### Splits in splits

Each level of lists divides the other way from the level that holds it.
This grid holds `a` beside a split of `b` above `c`:

```{r}
dock_grid("a", list("b", "c"))
```

```
┌──────────────┬──────────────┐
│              │      b       │
│      a       ├──────────────┤
│              │      c       │
└──────────────┴──────────────┘
```

A third level divides the way of the first, so this grid holds `a` above a split of `b` beside `c`:

```{r}
dock_grid(list("a", list("b", "c")))
```

```
┌─────────────────────────────┐
│              a              │
├──────────────┬──────────────┤
│      b       │      c       │
└──────────────┴──────────────┘
```

### Sizes

The argument `sizes` gives the share of each child of the top split:

```{r}
dock_grid("a", "b", sizes = c(0.3, 0.7))
```

```
┌────────┬────────────────────┐
│        │                    │
│   a    │         b          │
│        │                    │
└────────┴────────────────────┘
    30%            70%
```

The shares are positive numbers, which need not sum to 1, since the grid scales them to ratios that do.
So `sizes = c(3, 7)` gives the same grid.
The function `group()` writes a split with shares of its own, for a split inside another:

```{r}
dock_grid("a", group("b", "c", sizes = c(0.6, 0.4)), sizes = c(0.3, 0.7))
```

```
┌────────┬────────────────────┐
│        │         b          │  60%
│   a    │                    │
│        ├────────────────────┤
│        │         c          │  40%
└────────┴────────────────────┘
    30%            70%
```

## Rails

A rail holds panels on the left or right edge of a view, outside the splits, with a tab for each panel.
The function `rail()` writes one, which `dock_grid()` takes among its arguments, but which takes no share in its `sizes`:

```{r}
dock_grid(c("a", "b"), rail("c"))
```

```
┌───────────┬─────────────────────────┐
│           │ [a]  b                  │
│           ├─────────────────────────┤
│     c     │                         │
│           │            a            │
│ left rail │                         │
└───────────┴─────────────────────────┘
```

A rail sits on the left edge unless its `position` is `"right"`, and its `active` names the tab that it shows.
Its `size` is its width in pixels while it is open, 500 unless given, which fits a row of core's Edit board plugin on one line.
A rail with `collapsed = TRUE` shows its tabs alone, until the user opens it:

```{r}
dock_grid("a", rail("b", collapsed = TRUE), rail("c", "d", position = "right"))
```

```
┌───┬─────────────────┬───────────────┐
│ b │                 │ [c]  d        │
│   │                 ├───────────────┤
│   │        a        │               │
│   │                 │       c       │
│   │                 │  right rail   │
└───┴─────────────────┴───────────────┘
```

The board option `sync_rails` is on unless the board or the blockr option `sync_rails` turns it off, as `new_sync_rails_option(FALSE)` does for a board.
While it is on, a rail that the user opens or collapses opens or collapses on that edge of every view that has a rail there.

## Plugins' panels

A bare id names the card of a block, and so does `blk()`.
The function `plg()` names the panel of a plugin, by the name that the script gives the plugin in the board's `plugins`:

```{r}
board <- new_board(
  blocks = c(data = new_dataset_block("iris"), head = new_head_block()),
  links = new_link("data", "head"),
  plugins = list(
    new_dock_plugin(
      views = list(
        main = dock_view(dock_grid(c("data", "head"), rail(plg("edit"))))
      )
    ),
    edit = new_edit_board_plugin()
  )
)
```

The script gives core's Edit board plugin the name `edit`, and the left rail of the view `main` holds the plugin's panel.
A grid may name a plugin by the id of its class instead, as `plg("blockr.core-edit_board_plugin")`, without the plugin in `plugins`.
As `new_board()` builds the board, the dock names each plugin by the id of its class, as `board_views()` shows:

```{r}
board_views(board)
```

An app runs every plugin class that `available_plugins()` gives, unless its script narrows them in the `plugins` of `serve()`.
So an app runs core's Edit board plugin whether or not its board holds the plugin, and the script above gives the plugin in `plugins` only to name it.
As the dock starts, it drops from each view the panel of a plugin that the app does not run, or whose class has no UI, since it cannot draw that panel.

## Several views

A board has as many views as `views` gives:

```{r}
board <- new_board(
  blocks = c(
    data = new_dataset_block("iris"),
    head = new_head_block(),
    tail = new_head_block(direction = "tail")
  ),
  links = c(new_link("data", "head"), new_link("data", "tail")),
  plugins = list(
    new_dock_plugin(
      views = list(
        overview = dock_view(dock_grid("data", list("head", "tail"))),
        first_rows = dock_view("head"),
        both_ends = dock_view(
          list("head", "tail", plg("edit")),
          name = "Both ends"
        ),
        notes = dock_view(list())
      ),
      active = "first_rows"
    ),
    edit = new_edit_board_plugin()
  )
)
```

A view without a name is named after its id, as "First rows" for `first_rows`.
In place of a grid, a view may take the panels that it shows: a bare id, a character vector of ids, or a list of ids and panel references, as the view `both_ends` takes.
Such a view gets the default grid over its panels: the plugins' panels in one tab group, beside the blocks' panels in another.
A view that shows no panel takes none, as `notes` does, and says "Start by adding a panel", with a button that opens the panel picker.
A block may show in several views, as `head` does above, but a view shows each panel at most once.

The view `first_rows` is active, so the board opens on it.
Without `active`, the board opens on the first view of the views menu.
Where the URL of the page names a view by its id, as `?view=both_ends`, the dock makes that view active as it starts, so that a link reaches a view.
An id that names no view changes nothing.

## Folders

A folder groups views and other folders in the views menu, at any depth, and changes nothing that a view shows.
The function `dock_folder()` writes one, and `new_dock_plugin()` takes the folders in `folders`, each by its id:

```{r}
dock <- new_dock_plugin(
  views = list(
    overview = dock_view(dock_grid("data", list("head", "tail"))),
    first_rows = dock_view("head", folder = "rows"),
    last_rows = dock_view("tail", folder = "rows"),
    source = dock_view("data", folder = "inputs")
  ),
  folders = list(
    rows = dock_folder("Rows"),
    inputs = dock_folder("Inputs", folder = "rows")
  )
)

dock
```

A view or a folder sits in the folder whose id it names in `folder`, and at the top of the views menu where it names none.
In each folder, and at the top, the views come first and the folders after them, each in the order that the script gives.
The print shows the views menu as a tree, and then each view with its grid.
The user opens and closes a folder in the views menu.

The board option `view_tabs` shows the views as a line of tabs under the navbar, with a tab for each view and folder at the top of the views menu, and a folder's tab opens a menu of what the folder holds.
A script turns it on with `new_view_tabs_option(TRUE)` in the `options` of `new_board()`.

## What R refuses

The functions refuse a mistake as the script runs, naming each place:

```{r, error = TRUE}
new_dock_plugin(views = list(main = dock_view(dock_grid("a", rail("a")))))
```

The function `new_dock_plugin()` refuses a grid that places a panel twice, where a panel on a rail and in a tab group counts as twice.
It also refuses a view or folder that names a folder that `folders` lacks, a folder that sits in itself, through the folders that hold it, and an `active` that names a view that `views` lacks.
The functions `dock_grid()`, `group()` and `rail()` refuse a share that is not positive, and a rail's width below 0.

The dock plugin knows nothing of the board that holds it, so `new_board()` refuses what only the board can tell:

```{r, error = TRUE}
new_board(
  blocks = c(data = new_dataset_block("iris")),
  plugins = list(
    new_dock_plugin(views = list(main = dock_view(c("data", "head"))))
  )
)
```

It refuses a grid that names a block that the board lacks, and a `plg()` that names neither a plugin of the board's `plugins` nor a plugin class, by an id of the form `{pkg}-{id}`.
It refuses no such id, since a grid may name a plugin that the app runs without the board holding it.

## Reading the views of a board

The function `board_views()` reads the views of a board, each as `dock_view()` writes it, with its grid, and `active_view()` reads the id of the active view:

```{r}
names(board_views(board))
active_view(board)
view_name(board_views(board)[["first_rows"]])
view_blocks(board_views(board)[["overview"]])
```

The function `view_name()` reads the name of a view, and `view_blocks()` the ids of the blocks whose cards it shows.
A script builds one board from another with them, as `new_dock_plugin(views = board_views(board)["overview"])` takes one view of `board`.

The dock plugin holds the sections that each card shows as well, which `new_dock_plugin()` takes in `visible`, as `visible = list(head = "outputs")`.
A card without an entry shows both its inputs and its outputs, and `board_visible()` reads the entries of a board (see `?new_dock_plugin`).

## Cheat sheet

| Goal | Code |
|---|---|
| Two cards side by side | `dock_grid("a", "b")` |
| One above the other | `dock_grid(list("a", "b"))` |
| A top split that divides from top to bottom | `dock_grid("a", "b", orientation = "vertical")` |
| Two tabs of one tab group | `dock_grid(c("a", "b"))` |
| A tab group that shows its second tab | `dock_grid(panels("a", "b", active = "b"))` |
| A card beside a split of two | `dock_grid("a", list("b", "c"))` |
| Shares of 30% and 70% | `dock_grid("a", "b", sizes = c(0.3, 0.7))` |
| Shares inside a split | `dock_grid("a", group("b", "c", sizes = c(0.6, 0.4)))` |
| A plugin's panel on the left rail | `dock_grid("a", rail(plg("edit")))` |
| A collapsed rail on the right | `dock_grid("a", rail("b", position = "right", collapsed = TRUE))` |
| A view with the default grid | `dock_view(c("a", "b"))` |
| A view that shows nothing | `dock_view(list())` |
| A view in a folder | `dock_view("a", folder = "f")`, with `folders = list(f = dock_folder("F"))` |
| The view that the board opens on | `new_dock_plugin(views, active = "id")` |

The help pages hold the rest: `?dock_grid` for grids and rails, `?dock_view` for views and folders, `?new_dock_plugin` for the dock's state, `?plg` for panel references and `?board_views` for the readers.
